stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Unlike woodcut, in which the artist carves away everything that should not print, mezzotint starts from a copper plate roughened all over with a toothed rocking tool; inked at that stage, the plate would print as a solid, velvety black. The printmaker therefore works from dark to light, scraping and burnishing the burr flat wherever a highlight is ______ less ink and print as soft grays or, if polished completely, as bright white.
explanation: Cover the blank and test each side. "The printmaker therefore works from dark to light, scraping and burnishing the burr flat wherever a highlight is wanted" can stand alone as a sentence. So can "smoothed areas hold less ink and print as soft grays...", which has its own subject (areas) and verbs (hold, print). Two complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon, so you should choose B.

A.why: You put only a comma between two complete sentences, which is a comma splice. "Smoothed" looks like the start of a modifier describing the burnishing, but "areas hold" makes the second half a full sentence of its own.

C.why: You ran two complete sentences together with no punctuation. The long first clause makes "wanted smoothed areas" read like one phrase, but "smoothed areas hold less ink" starts a new sentence.

D.why: You were right to use a semicolon, but "holding" is not a main verb. That leaves "smoothed areas holding less ink and print as soft grays" as a fragment, which a semicolon cannot introduce, and "holding" no longer matches the verb "print" that follows.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The oral cholera vaccine is usually given as two doses spaced at least two weeks apart, a schedule that can be hard to complete during outbreaks among displaced people. To test a simpler approach, researchers in one large field trial gave participants just a single dose. That dose provided substantial protection to adults during the first several ______ protection was much weaker in children under five.
explanation: "That dose provided substantial protection to adults during the first several months" is a complete sentence, and so is "this protection was much weaker in children under five." The second sentence sets a limit on the first, so "however" belongs at the start of the second clause. The semicolon goes before it and a comma after it: "months; however, this."

A.why: You treated "however" like a conjunction that can join sentences. It can't. With commas on both sides of it, the two complete sentences are still joined by a comma alone, which is a comma splice.

B.why: The punctuation is correct, but "therefore" says the weaker protection in children happened because adults were protected. The real relationship is contrast: strong results in one group, weak results in another.

D.why: You left out all punctuation, so two complete sentences run together. The transition word does not replace the period or semicolon the break needs.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before lightweight geolocators were available, ornithologists assumed that Arctic terns flew roughly straight lines between Greenland and the Weddell Sea. Tags weighing barely more than a paper clip told a different story. The birds almost never take the most direct path between their breeding and wintering ______ prevailing wind systems, they trace a vast S-shaped route over the Atlantic that adds thousands of kilometers but costs them far less energy.
explanation: Read past the participle. "Following prevailing wind systems" is an introductory phrase, but the words after it, "they trace a vast S-shaped route," give the second half its own subject and verb. That makes the second half a complete sentence, and so is "The birds almost never take the most direct path between their breeding and wintering grounds." A period correctly separates them.

A.why: You read "following prevailing wind systems" as a modifier tacked onto the first sentence. Because "they trace" follows, the second half is a complete sentence, so the comma creates a comma splice.

B.why: You fused two complete sentences with no punctuation. "Grounds following prevailing wind systems" sounds like one phrase, but the subject "they" later shows that a new sentence has started.

C.why: Adding "and" without a comma doesn't fix the break. It turns "following" into an apparent partner of "take," and the sentence then collapses when "they trace" arrives. Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted a faint, recurring mark on the paper charts produced by a radio telescope near Cambridge, England. The pulses arrived about every 1.3 seconds, with a regularity that no known natural source seemed able to produce. Her team briefly nicknamed the signal LGM-1, half-joking that it might be a message from distant ______ later identified it as a pulsar: a collapsed star spinning rapidly and sweeping a beam of radio waves past Earth.
explanation: "Her team briefly nicknamed the signal LGM-1, half-joking that it might be a message from distant civilizations" is a complete sentence, and "astronomers later identified it as a pulsar" is another. The participle phrase "half-joking..." does not change that. A comma followed by the conjunction "but" correctly joins the two, and "but" fits the contrast between the joke and the real explanation.

B.why: You joined two complete sentences with a comma alone. The "half-joking" phrase already ends in a string of commas, so one more feels natural, but it is a comma splice.

C.why: You chose the right conjunction but dropped the comma it needs. When "but" joins two long complete sentences, the comma has to come before it.

D.why: "Having" turns the second half into "astronomers having later identified it," which has no main verb. After "but" you need a complete clause, and this is only a phrase.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Karst aquifers form where slightly acidic groundwater dissolves limestone over thousands of years, opening caves and conduits that can move water several kilometers in a single day. That speed makes karst springs abundant sources of drinking ______ also makes them vulnerable: a pesticide spilled in a field can reach a distant spring within hours, long before filtration through soil could remove it.
explanation: "That speed makes karst springs abundant sources of drinking water" is a complete sentence. "The same property also makes them vulnerable" is also complete, with subject "property" and verb "makes." A semicolon correctly joins two closely related complete sentences.

A.why: You used a comma alone between two complete sentences. The ideas are closely related, but a comma still can't join them without a conjunction like "but."

C.why: You left out punctuation, so two complete sentences run together. "Drinking water the same property" doesn't make sense as one phrase.

D.why: "Which" turns "also makes them vulnerable" into a relative clause, so "the same property" never gets a main verb. What follows the semicolon is then a fragment, and a semicolon must have a complete sentence on each side.
